extracted.intended_audience: readers and commentators of military reporting and media critics / journalists verifying battlefield accounts
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the credibility and accuracy of first‑person/military reporting (accounts of incidents in theater) with emphasis on journalistic fact‑checking, sourcing, and technical plausibility checks. Useful for bloggers, reporters, and readers scrutinizing claims about soldiers and contractors in combat zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: On‑the‑record sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Contacting experts for on‑the‑record discussions rather than relying on anonymous assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes running down claims by contacting experts for on‑the‑record discussions 'a level of transparency that Franklin Foer and The New Republic doesn't seem to want to provide.' Use identified, on‑the‑record sources to substantiate extraordinary claims; anonymous sourcing reduces credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for official reports/complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify whether there is a police report or formal complaint filed about the alleged incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major Renee D. Russo's emailed response notes 'There is not a police report or complaint filed on this incident during that timeframe.' Reporters should search official records and ask public affairs offices (PAOs) for documentation; absence of a report is a meaningful negative data point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek confirmation from local PAOs
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm whether military Public Affairs Offices at the relevant bases have records or were contacted prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post describes attempting to get verification from five PAOs in Kuwait to see if TNR had contacted them. Journalists should contact local PAOs to corroborate presence of personnel, incidents, and whether reporters made a good‑faith verification effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand documentary evidence for investigation conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that a military investigation refuted or disproved allegations, provide documentation supporting that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blogger promises to 'post any documentation as it becomes available.' If citing an investigation's result (e.g., 'refuted by members of his platoon'), attach or cite the investigative report, written statements, or other primary documents so readers can assess scope and specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing investigative findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise about which allegations were found false and which remain unverified or true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter notes ambiguity: 'Which allegation was determined to be false?... It only says one is false.' Don't imply that 'all allegations' were disproven when only one or some were; report the exact scope of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about sources of factual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: State how the author or source 'knew' a detail (e.g., IED caused the burns)—cite whether it was told to the author, assumed, or witnessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter observes Beauchamp gives no indication of how he came to 'know' the cause of the woman's injuries. Good reporting should explain provenance of factual claims (direct witness, medical record, told by another person, inference), so readers can judge reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check temporal and geographic consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that incidents occurred when and where the author claims (e.g., Kuwait vs FOB Falcon; before vs after deployment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post points out major timeline/location contradictions that undermine the story's narrative (incident moved to Kuwait and occurred before combat). Cross‑check unit deployment records, base rosters, and timelines to confirm location and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish status of subjects (contractor vs military)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurately identify whether involved persons were military personnel, contractors, or civilians and verify that status with records or PAOs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blogger and commenters highlight uncertainty whether the woman was 'military or contracter.' Misidentifying status affects expectations (evacuation, uniform rules) and investigative leads; reporters should confirm employment/status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by peers or unit members
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek corroboration or refutation from platoon mates, chain of command, or other people who served with the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites a quote: 'refuted by members of his platoon and proven to be false.' Peer corroboration (named when possible) can blunt or bolster first‑person narratives; however, prefer on‑the‑record named corroborators to anonymous claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on anonymous sources for extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on unnamed sources or anonymous 'experts'/'witnesses' when making serious accusations about conduct in theater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter states 'TNR has zero credibility to rely on anonymous sources *or* anonymous "experts" or "witnesses".' Extraordinary claims require identifiable corroboration; if anonymity is used, explain why and seek independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical plausibility checks with subject‑matter experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify technical or tactical claims (e.g., vehicle maneuvers, battlefield procedures) with people who have relevant hands‑on experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters (APC/Bradley/BFV drivers, Marines, vehicle mechanics) dispute the plausibility of described maneuvers. For technical assertions, consult specialists (vehicle drivers, armor crews, engineers) and report whether the claimed action is feasible and under what conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical/evacuation plausibility checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Check medical protocols and evacuation practices to see whether an injured person would have remained in theater or been evacuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter notes that 'anyone... injured / burned that badly would not have been allowed to remain in country' and would be transported to the US or Europe. Verify standard medical evacuation/treatment practices for the theater and time in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about corrections and narrative impact
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing corrections or 'minor' revisions, be transparent about what was changed and how it affects the overall narrative or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blogger anticipates 'minor correction' shifting facts (e.g., location or cause of burns). Outlets should clearly label corrections, describe their scope, and explain whether core conclusions are affected rather than burying them in vague edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for agenda‑driven framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to whether a work is being used to advance an editorial or political agenda rather than to accurately report facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post accuses TNR of using Beauchamp's words 'as a tool for their own agenda.' Readers and editors should separate factual verification from rhetorical framing; if a piece advances a predictable agenda, scrutinize the evidentiary basis more closely.
